kills.flaw: A shiny object that misses the mission by design. Revenue starts around month 10, it depends on a Bandai IP launch the user can't control (Lorcana-style cooling), and Bandai already runs official card databases for One Piece and Gundam. It can't reach $5-10k/month inside 12 months, and it pulls focus from the one test that matters.

Its own math puts it at about $1.5-2k/month net in year 1, with the payoff years away. Older collectors are slow and expensive to reach. As a standalone business it can't carry the user. It's only worth having later as a feature of the desk.

The math only works if Q4 Meta CAC stays under $35 against a $55 gross margin, and holiday CPMs reliably rise exactly then. Pokemon-trademark friction in ads is a second risk. demand-2 already covers the gift edge with better unit economics and uses free bulk.

upgrades.upgrade: Make it a refer-first ladder so a novice can't blow up. For the first 60 days, buy outright only cert-verifiable slabs and clearly identified lots under $1,500. Consign or refer all raw vintage and anything over $1,500 for a fee. Graduate to raw buys after 10 logged deals with realized margin at 30% or more. Keep a one-line decision journal per offer (predicted value vs realized) so calibration replaces gut feel. Pre-commit dated kill rules: after $1,000 of ad spend (about day 21), cost per qualified lead must be under $150, and by day 90 there must be 8 or more buys at $250+ net each.

Adopt marketing-1's 'dealer who shows you the receipts' report as the closer, and growth-1's liquidator finder's-fee channel as the free lead source. Then the desk doesn't depend on paid search alone.

The hook checks out: eBay moved US Promoted Listings General to 'any buyer clicked in the last 30 days' attribution on Jan 13, 2026 (ecomcrew, Value Added Resource). Launch it as a $149 Upwork productized audit on day 1, his home turf, and add mindset-1's Amazon accessory brands as a second customer profile. Kill rule: if 10 free audits produce fewer than 2 paid clients by Nov 15, stop. Run it as the zero-capital cash floor that pays the desk's ad tests.

Delay it to month 3-4, after the desk proves cost per qualified lead. A venue contract and insurance are closer to a one-way door than an ad test. Keep the excellent refundable pre-sale go/no-go (25+ paid tables by day 15). Add a 'free AI appraisal at the door' booth the user staffs himself, which turns every show into a collection-lead event for the desk.

Paying sellers 55-65% is a costly assumption for someone with no hobby experience. Start offers at about 50% and raise them only after realized margin is proven over 10 deals. Use the remote, small-lead edge (the $300-1,500 collections dealers won't drive to) as the positioning, not a higher payout.
A 65% close rate is optimistic. Model 35-40%, as the other variants do. Keep the side-by-side cash-vs-consign offer, which is the best trust mechanic on the board.

Run it only as a capped 30-day, $700 test fed by the desk's bulk, and only if it doesn't take Q4 hours from the desk's ad test. Otherwise it's a second business competing for a solo operator's 15-25 hours.
Don't order inventory until an arbitrage-1 or mindset-1 client gives first-hand category data (CVR, ACoS, return reasons). Learn on someone else's capital first, then launch your own SKU.
Make the report free and fold it into growth-1's liquidator channel as the partner offer. Selling $149-499 reports against dealers who appraise for free is the weak link.
Test the format with 10 pre-recorded 'what's in the shoebox' shorts from desk buys before committing to twice-weekly live shows. Go live only once one clip reaches 10k views.

combo: The Collection Desk Ladder. Engine: business-2 (buy / consign / refer every lead) with marketing-1's transparent receipts report and growth-1's liquidator finder's-fee channel as a free lead source. Run arbitrage-1 in parallel for the first 90 days as a zero-capital service income that pays for ad tests and protects the existing PPC work. Add business-1's show (with an appraisal booth) only after month 3 if desk economics validate. Guardrails: an $8k bankroll hard cap for 90 days, refer-first buying rules for a novice, and dated kill rules (after $1,000 of ads, cost per qualified lead must be under $150; by Dec 30, 2026, 8+ buys at $250+ net each). Smallest next step within 48 hours: Claude ships the intake page and the user turns on $40/day.
message: Nine of 27 ideas are the same collection-buying engine. That convergence is signal, but watch confirmation bias: the CPC data is real, while cost per qualified lead, the one number that decides this, is still a guess. It's a two-way door, so stop debating variants and spend $1,000 over 21 days to learn it, while a zero-capital service runs alongside. The real risk isn't the market. It's the user starving his working PPC income for the hobby's dopamine, so cap the bankroll and let the written kill rules make the call.
